questions.q: What are the two phases of the ring AllReduce algorithm, in order?
options: Broadcast, then reduce
Scatter-reduce, then all-gather
All-gather, then scatter-reduce
Reduce, then broadcast
questions.explain: Ring AllReduce first runs scatter-reduce, where each GPU ends up holding one fully-reduced piece of the result, then all-gather, where those pieces circulate so every GPU ends up with the complete result.

questions.q: Why is ring AllReduce described as 'bandwidth-optimal'?
options: Because it uses zero bandwidth
Because each GPU's total traffic approaches a constant (≈2S) as N grows, independent of the number of GPUs participating
Because it only works with exactly 2 GPUs
Because it eliminates the need for a network entirely
questions.explain: Per-GPU traffic in ring AllReduce is 2×(N-1)/N×S, which approaches a constant 2S as N grows large — meaning the data volume any single GPU must move doesn't increase just because more GPUs join the collective.

questions.q: What is the main drawback of the ring AllReduce algorithm at very large GPU counts?
options: It uses too much GPU memory
It requires 2(N-1) total sequential communication steps, and the fixed per-step latency overhead adds up at large N
It cannot be used with FSDP
It only works over Ethernet, never InfiniBand
questions.explain: Even though ring AllReduce's bandwidth cost per GPU stays flat, it requires 2(N-1) sequential steps. At very large N, the fixed latency overhead of each step accumulates, which is where tree-based algorithms become more attractive.

questions.q: How does a tree algorithm address ring AllReduce's weakness at scale?
options: It eliminates the need for any network bandwidth
It reduces the number of sequential steps to roughly log(N), trading a bit more bandwidth for lower latency
It only works for Broadcast operations, not AllReduce
It requires every GPU to be on the same physical node
questions.explain: Tree algorithms cut the number of sequential communication steps down to roughly log(N) instead of ring's 2(N-1), reducing latency at large scale at the cost of somewhat higher bandwidth usage. NCCL_ALGO controls which algorithm is selected.

questions.q: How does FSDP's use of ReduceScatter plus AllGather relate to a single ring AllReduce operation?
options: They are completely unrelated algorithms with no shared structure
ReduceScatter and AllGather together are structurally similar to splitting AllReduce's two phases apart across the forward and backward passes
AllGather replaces the need for any reduction operation in FSDP
ReduceScatter is only used for model inference, never training
questions.explain: Ring AllReduce's scatter-reduce phase mirrors ReduceScatter, and its all-gather phase mirrors AllGather. FSDP splits these two phases apart, using ReduceScatter for gradients and AllGather for parameters, effectively spreading one AllReduce's work across the training step.
